The two reciprocal pairs, A and B and C and D, are drawn in the accent color: four of the seven arcs have a partner pointing back, so reciprocity is 4 / 7 = 0.571." width="100%"} Reciprocity measures the proportion of edges in a directed graph that are bidirectional (mutual). Returns a value between `0.0` (no reciprocal edges) and `1.0` (all edges are reciprocal). This metric is fundamental for understanding relationship symmetry in social networks, mutual influence in citation networks, and bidirectional flows in transportation or communication networks. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["default"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How reciprocity is counted. With `"default"`, it is the share of edges whose reverse edge also exists, as in NetworkX. With `"ratio"`, it is the share of connected pairs of nodes that are joined both ways, as in igraph: each pair counts once, whether it is joined in one direction or both. A graph whose share of reciprocated edges is `r` has a ratio of `r / (2 - r)` (when it has no self-loops or parallel edges). Self-loops are ignored by `"ratio"`, and by both modes when finding mutual pairs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Reciprocity value between `0.0` and `1.0`, or `0.0` for empty graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on an undirected graph or with invalid mode. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~which_mutual`) : List the mutual pairs of edges. [](`~count_mutual_node_pairs`) : Count the pairs of nodes joined both ways. [](`~triadic_census`) : Count the patterns of edges among three nodes. [](`~density`) : The value that reciprocity would have by chance. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Of the three edges, two form a mutual pair, so the reciprocity is `2 / 3`. Counted by pairs of nodes instead, one of the two connected pairs is mutual: ::: {#ec7eeacd .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ben", "Ana"), ("Ana", "Cruz")], directed=True ) round(graph.reciprocity(), 3), graph.reciprocity(mode="ratio") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.667, 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ### More than chance `payments()` is a month of payments between 18 accounts at a made-up bank, each directed from payer to payee. `celegans_neural()` is the network of a worm's neurons that Watts and Strogatz used, and in `wiki_vote()` an edge runs from each Wikipedia user to every candidate they voted on in elections for administrators. If the edges were drawn at random, the chance that an edge is returned would be the density of the network, so the two are best read side by side. Wikipedia users vote on each other 28 times as often as chance, and the worm's neurons connect both ways 6 times as often. In the payments, the four returned payments are what chance alone would give: ::: {#13582e1b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl networks = { "payments": ec.payments(), "celegans_neural": ec.celegans_neural(), "wiki_vote": ec.wiki_vote(), } pl.DataFrame( { "network": list(networks), "reciprocity": [ round(g.reciprocity(), 3) for g in networks.values() ], "density": [round(g.density(), 4) for g in networks.values()], } ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
